# Agent B: managed sandbox discovery

Status: independent initial discovery complete, 2026-10-07. Candidate design only. No runtime experiment, installation, credential read, image operation, contact or canonical edit occurred. Initial conclusions were formed without reading other agents' reports.

## Conclusion

Managed sandboxes are credible execution substrates, but the inspected products do not establish the existing distributed filesystem and termination contract by documentation alone. Recommend testing Docker Cloud Sandboxes as an optional substrate using cold recovery through the retained SDK adapter and one persistent exclusive volume. Do not select memory snapshot restoration as the authoritative recovery mechanism. Docker's current cloud volume restrictions reject a naive combination of concurrent shared workspace mounts and memory snapshot restoration. This is a proposed deployment specialization, not approved adoption or a replacement executor.

If simultaneous mounting by segment and effect sandboxes is mandatory, reject Docker Cloud's inspected volume mode unless a supported alternative is established. The simplest candidate sequences ownership: finish and destroy segment execution, release its attachment, attach the same volume to an isolated effect environment, record outcome, destroy that environment, then resume in a fresh segment environment. This needs proof that attachment release and sandbox deletion stop every old actor; exclusive storage attachment alone does not prevent an old actor from sending network effects.

Confidence: high that the API contracts below are documented; medium that a thin substrate adapter is implementable; low that managed provider host loss and termination can yet satisfy all required guarantees. No deployment is qualified.

## Scope and existing evidence

The deployment application is greenfield by operator clarification relayed by the lead. Existing integration library and fixtures are brownfield reference dependencies. Proposed queues and Workers below are new topology, not inferred deployed topology. Historical maps are not current deployed application evidence.

Repository AGENTS.md and dirty Git status were read first. Published baseline is c79bdb516f4a4fe343bb97c1c97b39f0d796c450, branch design-base. The canonical location/checkpoint, spec, plan runtime contract, evidence references, work items, private README and ticket requirements were inspected. Current independent verification checkpoint supersedes historical paragraphs. Phase 1 bounded DONE dispositions remain unchanged. DSR-0.6 and DSR-0.11 remain owner decisions, rather than implementation permission.

Reuse the original pending recovery evidence and verified package/confinement controls described in verification-20261007.md. Selected SDK 0.2.162 / CLI 2.1.274 Linux/Python 3.13 installed controls passed 752 with 52 skipped; this does not prove a managed runtime. Minimum original recovery refusal remains accepted bounded evidence, not successful recovery. Synthetic injected-result callback closure remains DEFECT. Historical question parser/coordinator FAILs and incomplete billing remain preserved.

Dirty source identities are recorded in sources.md. No published clean-tree provenance is implied.

## Prior art and current capability findings

| Candidate | Evidence and maturity | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Docker local Sandboxes | Stable CLI release 0.47.0 dated 2026-10-05; local microVM persistence and host filesystem passthrough documented | Reference for isolation and local lifecycle; reject as standalone permanent host-loss solution |
| Docker Cloud Sandboxes API v1 | Experimental API, REST access available from Python, custom image supported, account enabled persistent volumes | Conditional reuse candidate for substrate; qualify exact API response schema, SDK/image digest and enabled features before experiments |
| Docker snapshot forks | Disk or memory modes documented, restore creates another identity | Reference for optional artifact capture; reject uncontrolled memory fork of active effect code |
| E2B | Managed persistence and snapshot APIs documented; snapshots require envd >=0.5.0; SDK 2.48.0 introduces stated refusal exception behavior; regional rollout caveats | Reference and fallback investigation candidate; do not assume infrastructure crash recovery from successful pause semantics |
| Daytona | Documentation displays v0.223; persistent shared volumes are S3 compatible object storage exposed through FUSE | Reference for artifact storage; reject claim-ledger selection until atomic exclusive create and visibility are proved |

Docker's local runtime retains guest data across stop/restart, but mounted workspace data remains on the host. Its local storage description does not promise protection from host/disk loss. [Architecture](https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes/architecture/)

Local and cloud stores, secrets and policy differ. Cloud does not expose host path mounts. `move` copies disk state, leaves the source, and transfers neither live process memory nor attached volumes. It is copying, not exclusive failover. [Local versus cloud](https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes/cloud/local-vs-cloud/)

Cloud volumes outlive sandbox deletion. Current recipe requires one exclusive attachment, release before transfer, and prohibits volume attachment to memory snapshot images. Durability after underlying host loss, fsync, UID behavior and exclusive file creation remain unestablished by this recipe. [Persistent storage](https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes-api/cookbook/attach-persistent-storage/)

Docker accepts custom registry images and REST requests. Running state does not establish completed kit setup; add image/engine/package readiness checks. Endpoint addresses can change. [API concepts](https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes-api/concepts/)

Creation/process mutations support replay keys, retained at least 24 hours. Persist original request and key before issuance; retain exact payload for retry. ETag preconditions protect resource mutations, not arbitrary filesystem effects. SDK automatic retries must be disabled or included in attempt accounting. A command wait timeout does not kill it. [Errors and retries](https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes-api/errors/)

Snapshot readiness is asynchronous. Capture of stopped sources is rejected; disk and memory modes exist. [Create snapshot contract](https://docs.docker.com/reference/api/sandboxes/latest/operations/createSnapshot/) Restoring a snapshot forks a new sandbox, rather than replacing the original. [Restore contract](https://docs.docker.com/reference/api/sandboxes/latest/operations/restoreSnapshot/)

Stop behavior can include hibernation when memory preservation is advertised. Therefore stopped does not necessarily mean all recorded execution state is discarded, and a later start may revive it. [Stop contract](https://docs.docker.com/reference/api/sandboxes/latest/operations/stopSandbox/) Prefer terminal deletion plus an independently observed termination oracle for handover.

E2B pause preserves disk and normally memory, whereas paused resources require explicit deletion. A refused pause may leave execution running and auto-pause backlog can fall back to filesystem-only restoration. Network clients must reconnect. These semantics are insufficient to use pause acknowledgement as our accepted segment commit. [Persistence](https://docs.e2b.dev/sandbox/persistence)

E2B snapshots leave the original running and support multiple offspring. They sever active client connections. Snapshot forks therefore need external run ownership and effect controls regardless of captured memory. [Snapshots](https://docs.e2b.dev/sandbox/snapshots)

Daytona volumes can be shared among sandboxes, but object storage presented as directories does not establish the filesystem properties our claims require. [Volumes](https://www.daytona.io/docs/en/volumes/)

## Complete candidate architecture

1. A new application Workflow maintains run lineage, accepted generation, pending identity, bounded decisions/outcomes and deployment receipt references. It stores references and hashes rather than raw transcript/archive content.
2. Proposed prepare, segment, effect and lifecycle Activities invoke existing package preparation, runner, adapter and supervisor responsibilities. Proposed queue names are deployment choices, not discovered existing queues. Sandbox lifecycle networking stays inside Activities.
3. Prepare registers immutable image digest, SDK/CLI/policy identity and validated package. Provision a run-scoped persistent volume with protected run root, read only package/settings/claims for script identity, effect writable work subtree. Whether provider volume permissions support this is a gate.
4. A host lifecycle adapter persists the exact create request and replay key before requesting a sandbox. Reconcile lost responses with the same key and poll immutable identity. Do not infer failure from client timeout.
5. The segment sandbox runs the retained Python SDK/controller entrypoint. It persists transcript/session and workspace state to the volume through the existing adapter and produces an immutable manifest bound to lineage, generation, pending call, source versions and state hashes. Native direct shell remains disabled.
6. Acceptance requires manifest validation and recorded segment result in Workflow state. Stop and terminally remove segment sandbox, observe attachment release and termination. If termination is uncertain, park and do not run an effect or replacement.
7. For effects, attach volume to an effect sandbox with no Worker/model credentials. Reuse existing external effect Activity after accepted commit. Write protected ordinal claim before arbitrary Bash spawn; enforce one attempt, timeout, descendant termination and definitive outcome persistence. Unknown outcome parks. Package and protected root remain unwritable by effects.
8. Destroy effect environment and verify teardown. A replacement segment mounts the volume, verifies accepted manifest against protected claims/outcomes, and resumes the exact original pending request/result through the retained adapter. Never substitute synthetic-result resume or normal CLI conversation resume.
9. Human wait happens in Workflow state with no executing sandbox. Durable signed decision binds lineage/generation/pending identity; its result is delivered only after original segment commit. Duplicate/conflicting answer and late stale generation are refused.
10. Janitor removes resources only after ownership is terminal and retention owner approves a horizon covering reset/replay/uncertainty. Unknown horizon keeps claims. Snapshot and volume cleanup are distinct from sandbox cleanup.

Transfer remains cold recovery, using durable application/session data. No promise to preserve transient streamed tokens or active provider connections. Candidate recovery point is the last accepted manifest. No numerical recovery time or loss target is invented; measurements must distinguish queue delay, sandbox allocation, mount/readiness, validation and SDK recovery.

## State authority and recovery contract

| State | Authority and storage | Acknowledgement/consistency/identity | Restore or missing state behavior |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Orchestration/outcomes | Workflow history and bounded carried state | Accepted Activity result / signed Update; lineage + generation + effect ordinal | Replay Workflow; never infer effect outcome from guest transcript |
| Session trajectory/checkpoint | Retained adapter in protected durable volume or approved store | Persist acknowledgement and immutable hash manifest; exact call/result JSON | Verify selected engine compatibility; missing/stale checkpoint refuses |
| Package/policy | Validated package manifest and immutable image identity | Package body hash + engine/SDK/policy version | Recreate same qualified package; forged name/version refuses |
| Workspace | Run volume, only work subtree effect writable | Persistence boundary must be measured; workspace manifest | Corrupt/partial/old restore refuses; never declare transcript alone sufficient |
| Claims/uncertainty | Protected run root plus Workflow outcome record | Proven exclusive create + durable flush; lineage + ordinal | Missing unresolved claim refuses; never rebuild empty claims to bypass uncertainty |
| Ownership/receipts | Workflow accepted ownership and lifecycle provider receipt | Sandbox immutable ID/incarnation and terminal teardown; no renewal after transfer | Unknown old owner parks; ETag is not host fencing proof |
| Credentials/keys | External deployment secret authority, scoped injection | Approved role and access policy; never package writable | Replacement gets approved credentials only; no copied expired memory token |

Retention is owner selected, at least sufficient for permitted replay/reset and effect uncertainty. Vendor idempotency replay window is not a substitute for retention of our claims and lifecycle records. Any cross-store write gap is visible: an orphan manifest before Workflow acceptance cannot dispatch effects; accepted manifest missing from storage parks; outcome saved before Activity completion is reused; effect completion without outcome remains uncertain.

Temporal cancellation is cooperative and depends on Activity communication. Activity timeout drives retries but does not itself kill sandbox code. Preserve one-attempt arbitrary effect policy and use lifecycle reconciliation rather than rerunning uncertain work. [Activity execution](https://docs.temporal.io/activity-execution)

## Capability matrix

| Capability | Status | Qualification needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exact original pending SDK recovery | Locally demonstrated bounded Phase 1 | Run same adapter inside selected managed substrate |
| Validated Skill confinement | Locally demonstrated bounded Phase 1 | Mount/permissions must preserve boundary |
| Custom image + command launch | Documented Docker API | Pinned image ready probe through mandatory SDK |
| Persistent reattachment | Documented | Real delete/reattach plus persistence/fsync proof |
| Concurrent volume sharing | Unsupported in inspected Docker cloud recipe | Change requirement or choose another substrate |
| Memory snapshot plus attached volume | Unsupported in inspected Docker cloud recipe | Reject this combination |
| Exclusive file claims across hosts | Untested | Real volume rig; attach exclusive does not establish O_EXCL semantics |
| Permanent provider host loss | Untested | Provider fault rig or contractual evidence plus targeted experiment |
| Authoritative descendant death/fencing | Untested | Independent canary and stale owner controls |
| Confidential execution | Not established by inspected managed sources | Separate provider/attestation selection |
| Billing, retention, region availability | Owner decision / unverified | Approved deployment/allowance and feature availability |

## Failure traces and falsifiable tests

All tests are PREPARED concepts, not executed commands. Topology T: selected managed backend version/region recorded, immutable existing fixture image imported only after approval, SDK 0.2.162 / CLI 2.1.274, persistent exclusive run volume, two independent controller Workers, existing original pending adapter, external deterministic effect sink that records run/ordinal and every physical request, and separate lifecycle canary receiver. Use synthetic model protocol fixture first; real model only separately approved. Never store provider credentials in test logs.

Common oracle: record immutable resource IDs, ETags, request hash/key, manifests, storage readbacks, Workflow history, claim/outcome hash and timestamped sink/canary counts. Failure is any effect before accepted commit, malformed resume, duplicate ordinal spawn, stale owner continuation, lost accepted state, or falsely successful cleanup. Cleanup terminally deletes all sandboxes, verifies sink/canary silence and provider disappearance, preserves retained claims, then deletes only disposable storage with approval. If terminal proof fails, stop the batch.

| Test | Fault and expected result | Evidence / limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| B1 process/container failure | Kill SDK process, then destroy sandbox before/after session persistence acknowledgement; replacement admits only verified accepted checkpoint | Session hash and expected pending identity; no streamed-token guarantee |
| B2 accepted segment boundary | Kill controller immediately before/after accepted segment commit | Before: zero effect; after: exactly eligible original pending dispatch. Workflow history + sink count |
| B3 claim boundary | Kill effect execution immediately before/after claim creation and immediately before/after spawn | Before claim: eligible one attempt; after claim with no outcome: parked, never another spawn. Independent sink counts |
| B4 effect/result boundary | Kill immediately before/after effect completion and durable outcome save | Saved outcome reused byte exactly; unsaved completion parked. Duplicate request is failure |
| B5 pending recovery boundary | Kill before/after original result injection/readback | Retained call/result unchanged; no duplicate effect, no fabricated question answer |
| B6 ownership transfer | Drop lifecycle response before/after deletion and attachment release; start two replacement controllers | Same create key recovers one resource; transfer blocked until terminal proof; at most one accepted owner |
| B7 host temporary partition | Disconnect controller from sandbox while canary continues | No replacement/effect until termination evidence; timeout alone must not release owner |
| B8 permanent host loss | Provider fault destroys host/local disk, independently durable volume survives | New placement recovers accepted state; provider resource receipt alone cannot prove real host loss; host injection unavailable means pending |
| B9 storage outage/partition | Deny or delay storage reads/writes and durability acknowledgement | No accepted manifest/effect from incomplete writes; bounded refusal/park; test actual provider volume not only mocks |
| B10 stale/partial restore | Restore older checkpoint or omit claim while retaining newer Workflow generation | Refuse before SDK/model/effect; preserve uncertain ordinal. Snapshot timestamp alone insufficient |
| B11 guest kernel and children | Crash guest; orphan/detach child that emits canary, then cancel/delete | No canary after terminal receipt; parent exit or process signal alone cannot pass |
| B12 compatibility | Change CLI/package/policy/image identity during replacement | Refuse before SDK; no implicit latest promotion |
| B13 human wait race | Accept answer during container/host failure; duplicate then conflicting answer | One durable accepted answer bound to original pending request, delivered only after commit; no sandbox held during wait |
| B14 retention | Attempt cleanup with parked effect and unknown horizon, then expired replay key | Claims retained; unknown lifecycle creation beyond replay window parks, not new key recreation |
| B15 snapshot fork negative | Restore two active-memory descendants from same snapshot | Neither may acquire original run execution; uncontrolled cloned network effect demonstrates rejection of memory-authoritative design |

B1 through B6 protocol/fault-ordering portions can be implemented as offline controls using existing fixtures, but new managed lifecycle integration is not implemented here. None supplies managed provider proof offline. B7 through B11 need actual sandbox and controllable storage/provider fault capability. B8 cannot be substituted by deleting a sandbox. All need separate execution scope, compute/storage allowance, account feature access and cleanup authority. Live model qualification follows only after deterministic lifecycle/storage proofs. No copied old live command or consumed reservation may be reused.

## Risks and decisive questions

| Assumption | Risk if wrong | Retirement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Provider deletion implies descendants cannot execute | Old and replacement both produce effects | B6/B7/B11 plus provider termination contract |
| Exclusive volume release follows actual execution death | Attachment transfers while old code still sends requests | Same tests; park without independent proof |
| Volume acknowledged writes survive host loss | Accepted checkpoint/claims vanish | B8/B9 and explicit storage durability specification |
| Snapshot includes mounted data consistently | New trajectory with stale workspace/claims | B10; do not use snapshot as authority |
| Image can preserve read only package/protected state | Effect alters package/claim or reads Worker credentials | Negative mount/identity/environment tests |
| API replay horizon covers recovery | Lost create beyond 24h becomes duplicate | B14; protected lifecycle journal and owner decision |
| Host injection is available to us | A successful happy path masquerades as host failure proof | Record B8 pending, narrow advertised scope |

New integration is limited to a substrate binding of existing host supervisor operations to API lifecycle, request journaling/readiness checks, run volume ownership transfer, and durable manifest validation. No new agent loop or execution semantics. Work cannot begin until operator selects deployment scope/security owner/storage and approves any specialization from simultaneous shared mounts to sequential exclusive mounts.

Strongest counterargument: the provider hides its hosts and gives us an API resource, not an authoritative local PID-zero receipt. If its terminal API semantics cannot be tied to old execution impossibility and host-loss durability, we cannot advertise transparent host failure continuation. Self managed infrastructure may be necessary despite managed convenience.

Smallest decisive experiment: B6 combined with deterministic B1/B3 on one persistent volume. Prove delete/release/reattach preserves protected claim and original pending session, lost create response reuses one identity, and a disconnected orphan cannot survive a terminal deletion receipt. No model request is necessary. Passing that still leaves actual host loss and storage durability pending.

Single next action: compare this independent report with the other candidates, challenge the termination and storage evidence, and select the first deterministic substrate qualification experiment for operator review.
